title: Supine and periphrastic conjugations

objectives.can: Recognise the supine after verbs of motion and in set phrases, and the two periphrastic conjugations.

explanation.summary: Three small constructions finish the verbal system. The supine is a rare verbal noun that gives purpose after a verb of motion, or respect after an adjective. The active periphrastic (future participle + *sum*) says what someone is about to do. The passive periphrastic (gerundive + *sum*) says what must be done or is to happen.

sections.heading: The supine in -um: purpose after motion
body: The supine is a fourth-declension noun of action with only two forms, and both are built from the same base as the perfect passive participle. The form in *-um* (accusative) follows a verb of going or sending and gives the purpose: 'went to bed', 'went to bathe'.

The clearest cases in these texts are three. In Genesis 19:4 the men of the city surrounded the house *prius quam irent cubitum*, 'before they went to bed'. In Augustine, *visum est mihi ut irem lauatum*, 'it seemed good to me to go to bathe'. In Tertullian, the question is whether John *miserit sciscitatum*, 'sent to enquire'. In each, the supine follows *ire* or *mittere* and says why.

The supine has no subject or tense of its own, and in the Vulgate it is rare. Purpose after a verb of motion is usually written with an infinitive (as in Luke 8:35, *Exierunt autem videre quod factum est*, 'they went out to see what had happened'), or with *ut*, or with *ad* and a gerundive, as the last lesson showed. The supine in *-um* also stands after *do* and *trado* in a few phrases, as in Matthew 24:38 *nuptum tradentes*, 'giving in marriage'.

sections.heading: The supine in -u: respect
body: The ablative form in *-u* follows an adjective and says in what respect the adjective is true: 'fair to see'. In Genesis 2:9 the trees are *pulchrum visu*, and in Isaiah 2:16 all that is *visu pulchrum*. In Lamentations 2:4 it is *omne quod pulchrum erat visu*. In 1 Maccabees 13:27 Simon builds a monument *altum visu*, 'lofty to the sight'.

The line between this supine and an ordinary fourth-declension noun in the ablative is thin, and grammarians draw it in different places. Compare 1 Samuel 17:42, where David is *pulcher aspectu*: *aspectu* is a noun, 'in appearance', and the sense is the same. The automatic analysis marks 21 words as supines in *-u*, but several of them are plain nouns used in the ablative, such as *ornatu*, *fluxu* and *rogatu*. Read the sense, not the label.

sections.heading: The active periphrastic: about to
body: The future participle (stem of the supine + *-urus*) with a form of *sum* is the active periphrastic conjugation. It says that someone is about to do something, is going to, or intends to. The participle is nominative and agrees with the subject; *sum* supplies the tense.

In Acts 12:6, *Cum autem producturus eum esset Herodes* means 'when Herod was about to bring him out'. The imperfect subjunctive *esset* places the intention in the past. In John 11:51 Caiaphas prophesied that Jesus *moriturus erat pro gente*, 'was going to die for the nation'. In Mark 14:30 Jesus says *tu ... me es negaturus*, 'you are going to deny me'. In Matthew 11:14 *Elias qui venturus est* is 'Elijah who is to come'.

It is not the same as the plain future. The periphrastic stresses the nearness or the intention, and it is the only way to put a future in the past, 'was about to', or in a subordinate clause that depends on a past verb: *sperabamus quia ipse esset redempturus Israël* (Luke 24:21), 'we hoped that he was going to redeem Israel'.

sections.heading: The passive periphrastic: must be, is to be
body: The gerundive with *sum* is the passive periphrastic. It expresses obligation or what is to happen, and the person who must act stands in the dative of agent. In Augustine, God is the one *qua solus colendus est*: 'by which he alone must be worshipped'. In Cassian, *Quinto nobis certamine ... stimuli retundendi sunt* means that in the fifth contest the stings of sadness must be blunted by us; *nobis* names the doers.

The tense is carried by *sum*. In 1 Peter 5:1 the glory is *quæ in futuro revelanda est*, 'which is to be revealed in the future'. In Galatians 3:23 it is *fidem quæ revelanda erat*, 'the faith that was to be revealed'. The same participle with *erat* moves the whole thing into the past.

A verb that has no passive subject can still be used. Then the gerundive is neuter singular and impersonal, and nothing in the sentence agrees with it. In Tertullian, *nobis gratulandum est* means 'we must rejoice', literally 'it is to be rejoiced by us'. In Augustine's Confessions, some people see *quo eundum sit*, 'where one must go', while others do not see the way. The analysis marks *eundum* there as a gerund, but this use, a gerundive of an intransitive verb with *sum*, is the impersonal passive periphrastic.

misunderstandings: Taking a supine for an accusative noun. In *irent cubitum* the word names an action, 'to go to bed', and the library files the form as a noun meaning 'cubit' only because the shape is the same.
Translating the active periphrastic as a simple future. It is stronger: 'is about to', 'was going to', 'is to'. With *erat* or *esset* it points to a time after a past moment.
Making the dative with a passive periphrastic the one who receives. *nobis colendus* or *nobis curandus* means 'to be cared for by us': *nobis* is the doer.

Treating every future participle with *sum* as the active periphrastic. A future participle can also stand alone as an adjective, as in *qui venturus est*; only the participle with a form of *sum* makes the conjugation.

deeper.heading: Why the supine is so thin in the Latin Bible
body: In classical prose the supine is already restricted: a few verbs of motion, a few adjectives. In the Latin Bible the first use is very rare, and purpose after motion is written in other ways. Where the Greek has an infinitive of purpose, the Latin tends to have an infinitive. Greek has no supine, so there was no Greek model to copy.
The periphrastic conjugations are more at home. The Vulgate uses the active periphrastic freely, and for the Greek 'is to come' and 'is about to' it uses *venturus est* and *moriturus erat*.

examples.analysis: *exisse deambulatum in hortos*: The speaker tells that, while the emperor was kept at the games, he and some companions had *exisse*, 'gone out', *deambulatum*, 'to walk'. *deambulatum* is a supine in *-um* after the verb of motion *exisse*, and gives the purpose. The library tags the form as a perfect participle, but there is no noun for a participle to agree with.

quoted.title: Acts
quoted.english: And when Herod would have brought him forth, the same night Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains: and the keepers before the door kept the prison.

options: Herod ought to bring him out
Herod had already brought him out
Herod was about to bring him out
check.explain: The future participle with *esse* is the active periphrastic, 'about to'. With the imperfect subjunctive *esset* in a *cum* clause the sense is 'when Herod was about to bring him out'.

options: That Jesus was to die: he was going to die for the nation
That Jesus was dying at that moment
That Jesus had died for the nation
check.explain: *moriturus* is a future participle, and *erat* places the prophecy in the past. The pair means 'was going to die'. It states what was ahead, not an obligation.

check.prompt: *ter me es negaturus* (words 18–21): how is *es negaturus* best translated?

quoted.title: Mark
quoted.english: And Jesus saith to him: Amen I say to thee, today, even in this night, before the cock crow twice, thou shall deny me thrice.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

check.explain: The future participle *negaturus* agrees with *tu* and *es* completes the active periphrastic. Jesus names what Peter is about to do; he does not give an order.

check.prompt: *fidem quæ revelanda erat* (words 10–14): what does *revelanda erat* mean?

quoted.title: Galatians
quoted.english: But before the faith came, we were kept under the law shut up, unto that faith which was to be revealed.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

check.explain: *revelanda* is a gerundive agreeing with *quæ* (the faith), and *erat* puts it in the past: the faith was still to be revealed. A passive periphrastic often says only what lay ahead.

options: That he alone is to be worshipped
That he has been worshipped alone
That he is worshipped by no one
check.explain: A gerundive with *est* is a passive periphrastic of obligation: he alone is to be worshipped. *colendus* is nominative masculine and agrees with the implied subject.

options: A relative clause with sit in a perfect
An active periphrastic: 'where he will go'
An impersonal passive periphrastic: 'where one must go'
check.explain: *eo* has no passive subject, so the gerundive is neuter and impersonal. With *sit* it says what must be done: where one has to go. The subjunctive is that of an indirect question.

reading.why: Caiaphas's words about one man dying for the people: a *quia* clause, the active periphrastic in *Jesus moriturus erat pro gente*, and a purpose clause with *ut*, in four short verses that also review the reported statement of the first lesson.
